hooks: Dakota is the Sioux word for "friend" or "ally" — the people’s own name for themselves.
It was split from South Dakota in 1889, and the two were admitted on the same day with the papers shuffled so nobody knows which was 39th and which 40th.
The Bakken shale under it made it briefly the second-largest oil producer in the country, and its population grew after a century of decline.
The only state named after a president — and it was nearly called Columbia, changed to avoid confusion with the District of Columbia.
That change failed entirely: people say Washington State to this day to avoid exactly that confusion.
Mount St Helens here lost 400 m of its summit in 1980 in the deadliest eruption in US history.
From Spanish montaña, "mountain" — chosen by a congressman who liked the sound of it.
The fourth largest state with the third lowest population density; it has more cattle than people.
Custer was killed at the Little Bighorn here in 1876, and Glacier National Park has lost most of the glaciers it was named for.
From Dakota mni sota, "sky-tinted water" or "cloudy water", for the Minnesota river.
It calls itself the land of 10,000 lakes and actually has about 11,842.
The Mississippi rises here at Lake Itasca, narrow enough to step across.
A made-up word: a lobbyist claimed it was Shoshone for "gem of the mountains", then admitted he had invented it — but the name had stuck.
It grows about a third of all US potatoes, in volcanic soil watered by the Snake River.
Hells Canyon on its border is the deepest river gorge in North America, deeper than the Grand Canyon.
Probably from the French province of Maine, or simply from "the main" — sailors’ shorthand for the mainland as against the islands.
The most forested state, about 89% trees, and it produces nearly all the wild blueberries in the country.
Its coastline is 5,600 km once the inlets are counted, longer than California’s.
From Ojibwe mishigami, "large water" — for the lake.
The only state in two separate pieces, joined by a five-mile bridge over the Straits of Mackinac.
It touches four of the five Great Lakes, and no point in it is more than 137 km from one.
From a Miami word recorded by the French as Meskousing, probably "river running through a red place"; the spelling drifted to Wisconsin.
It makes about a quarter of all American cheese, and its residents are called cheeseheads without embarrassment.
The Republican Party was founded in Ripon here in 1854, and the state pioneered workers’ compensation and unemployment insurance.
The same Dakota — "friend" in Sioux — as its northern twin.
Mount Rushmore was carved between 1927 and 1941 into a mountain sacred to the Lakota, whose claim to the Black Hills the Supreme Court upheld in 1980.
They refused the compensation, which now sits accruing interest at over a billion dollars, because accepting it would confirm the sale.
Origin genuinely unknown: possibly from a French map’s mislabelled "Ouaricon-sint", or from a Spanish or Algonquian word.
Crater Lake here is the deepest lake in the United States at 594 m, filling the caldera of a collapsed volcano.
It has no sales tax, and by law you could not pump your own petrol in most of the state until 2023.
Named in 1629 after the English county of Hampshire by a captain who had lived there.
Its presidential primary has gone first in the nation since 1920, which is written into state law.
The Old Man of the Mountain, its stone-face emblem, collapsed in 2003 — the state kept it on the licence plates.
From French vert mont, "green mountain" — the name of the Green Mountain Boys who fought for its independence.
It was an independent republic from 1777 to 1791, with its own currency and postal service.
The first state to abolish adult slavery in its constitution, in 1777, and it has no billboards by law.
From a Delaware phrase, xwé:wamənk, "at the big river flat" — a Pennsylvania valley name transplanted 2,000 km west.
The least populous state, with fewer people than several American cities.
It gave women the vote in 1869, half a century before the nation, and Yellowstone here was the world’s first national park.
Named in 1664 for the Duke of York, later James II, when the English took New Amsterdam from the Dutch.
The Erie Canal, opened in 1825, linked the Hudson to the Great Lakes and made New York the busiest port in the country.
Its Adirondack Park is larger than Yellowstone, Yosemite, Grand Canyon and Glacier combined, and is constitutionally "forever wild".
From the Massachusett people: "at the great hill", probably the Blue Hills near Boston.
Harvard, founded 1636, is the oldest university in the country, and the first American public school and first subway are both here.
It was the first state to legalise same-sex marriage, in 2004.
Named for the Ioway people, whose own name may come from a word meaning "sleepy ones" given by neighbours.
It has about a quarter of the best-grade farmland in the country and grows more corn than any other state.
Its caucuses opened the presidential nominating season for half a century.
Probably from Dutch roodt eylandt, "red island", for its clay — or from a supposed likeness to Rhodes.
The smallest state, and the one with the longest official name: it was "the State of Rhode Island and Providence Plantations" until 2020.
It was founded by Roger Williams as a refuge for religious dissenters, and had the first Baptist church and the oldest synagogue in America.
From Mohegan quinnitukqut, "at the long tidal river".
Its 1639 Fundamental Orders are sometimes called the first written constitution in the Western world, which is why it is the Constitution State.
Hartford has been the insurance capital of America since the 1800s, starting with fire policies.
From Otoe ñí braðke or Omaha ni btháska, "flat water" — the Platte river, which is exactly that.
The only state with a unicameral, officially nonpartisan legislature.
Its Sandhills are the largest sand dune area in the Western Hemisphere, held in place by grass.
"Penn’s woods" — but named for William Penn’s father; Penn himself was embarrassed and tried to have it changed.
The Declaration of Independence and the Constitution were both signed in Philadelphia.
It is officially a Commonwealth, as are Virginia, Massachusetts and Kentucky, which means nothing legally.
From Seneca ohi:yo’, "good river" or "large creek".
Eight presidents were born here, more than any state except Virginia, which is why it is called the Mother of Presidents.
The Wright brothers were from Dayton, and both Neil Armstrong and John Glenn were Ohioans.
Named for the Channel Island of Jersey, home of one of the colony’s proprietors.
The most densely populated state, and it has more diners than anywhere else in the country.
Edison’s Menlo Park lab here produced the phonograph and the practical light bulb, and the first baseball game was played in Hoboken.
"Land of the Indians", coined for a land company in 1768 — a name given by settlers, not by the people it names.
Its 500-mile race has run at the Brickyard since 1911.
It has more miles of interstate per square mile than any other state, which is why it calls itself the Crossroads of America.
From the Illinois Confederation, through French — the -ois ending is a French spelling, which is why the s is silent.
Chicago’s 1871 fire led to the rebuilding that produced the world’s first skyscraper in 1885.
It produces more soybeans and nuclear power than any other state.
From the Ute people; the name may mean "people of the mountains".
The Great Salt Lake in it is the largest lake west of the Mississippi and saltier than the ocean.
About 62% of its people are Mormon, and Salt Lake City was founded in 1847 by settlers who walked there.
Named for the Delaware river, itself named for Lord De La Warr, a colonial governor — the Lenape people were then renamed after him too.
The first state to ratify the Constitution, in 1787, which is why it is called the First State.
More than half of all US public companies are legally incorporated here, for its courts and its corporate law.
Spanish for "coloured red", for the silt in the Colorado river.
It has more land above 3,000 m than any other state, and its lowest point is higher than the highest point in eighteen others.
Its border is drawn entirely with straight lines, though survey errors left it with 697 sides rather than four.
It split from Virginia in 1863 rather than leave the Union — the only state formed by seceding from a seceding state.
Almost entirely mountainous, with the highest average elevation east of the Mississippi.
The Hatfield-McCoy feud ran along its Kentucky border, and coal mining shaped both its economy and its politics.
Columbia is a poetic name for America, from Columbus; the district was carved from Maryland and Virginia to belong to no state.
Its residents had no presidential vote until 1961 and still have no voting member of Congress — hence the licence plates reading "taxation without representation".
No building may rise above a 1910 height limit, which is why the city stays low and the Capitol still dominates.
For Henrietta Maria, queen of Charles I — one of several colonies named for a monarch’s wife.
The Star-Spangled Banner was written here during the 1814 bombardment of Fort McHenry.
The Chesapeake Bay in it is the largest estuary in the country, and its blue crabs are a state institution.
Spanish for "snow-covered", from the Sierra Nevada on its western edge — which is odd for the driest state in the country.
The federal government owns about 80% of it, more than any other state.
Gambling was legalised in 1931 during the Depression, and the Hoover Dam was built the same decade.
From the Kansa people, whose name means "people of the south wind".
It is measurably flatter than a pancake, by an actual study that compared both.
Its 1954 Brown v. Board of Education case ended legal school segregation across the country.
From a Siouan word meaning "those who have dugout canoes", the name Illinois people used for their neighbours.
The Gateway Arch in St Louis marks where westward expansion began; the Oregon, Santa Fe and California trails all started in this state.
The 1857 Dred Scott case that helped precipitate the Civil War was filed in St Louis.
For Elizabeth I, the Virgin Queen — the oldest English place name in America, given in 1584.
Eight presidents were born here, more than any other state, and four of the first five.
Jamestown in 1607 was the first permanent English settlement, and the Civil War ended at Appomattox in this state.
From an Iroquoian word, probably kentá:ke, "on the meadow" — not, as often claimed, "dark and bloody ground".
Mammoth Cave here is the longest cave system in the world, with over 680 km mapped and no end found.
It makes about 95% of the world’s bourbon, which must by law be aged in new charred oak.
From a fictional island in a 1510 Spanish romance, ruled by a black queen called Calafia — explorers thought the peninsula was that island.
If it were a country it would have one of the largest economies in the world.
It holds both the highest and lowest points in the contiguous states, Mount Whitney and Death Valley, 135 km apart.
From Tanasi, a Cherokee town on the Little Tennessee river; the meaning is not known.
It borders eight states, tied with Missouri for the most.
Memphis and Nashville between them produced blues, rock and roll and country; Sun Studio recorded Elvis, Cash and Presley’s first single.
From Choctaw okla humma, "red people" — proposed by a Choctaw chief for the Indian Territory.
Sixty-seven tribes were relocated here, many along the Trail of Tears, and it has the second-largest Native American population.
The 1889 land runs opened it to settlers who raced for claims; those who slipped in early were called Sooners.
Carolina is from Carolus, Latin for Charles — for Charles I, and later confirmed for Charles II.
The Wright brothers flew at Kitty Hawk here in 1903, choosing it for the steady wind and soft sand.
Its Outer Banks are barrier islands that shift, and the graveyard of the Atlantic offshore has wrecked over a thousand ships.
From a French rendering of a Quapaw name — which is why it is pronounced like Kansas’s neighbour but spelled with a silent s.
The Crater of Diamonds here is the only diamond mine in the world where the public may dig and keep what they find.
Walmart was founded in Bentonville in 1962 and is now the largest company in the world by revenue.
Probably from O’odham alĩ ṣon-ak, "small spring", through Spanish Arizonac.
The Grand Canyon is 446 km long and up to 1,857 m deep, cut by the Colorado over millions of years.
It does not observe daylight saving time, except on the Navajo Nation, which does.
Named by Spaniards in the 1560s, decades before there was a country called Mexico — so it is not "new" anything.
The first atomic bomb was detonated at Trinity here in July 1945, and Los Alamos designed it.
It has the highest share of Hispanic residents of any state, and Santa Fe is the oldest capital city in the country, from 1610.
The other half of Carolus, split from the north in 1712.
The Civil War began here when Confederate guns fired on Fort Sumter in Charleston harbour in April 1861.
Its Gullah communities on the Sea Islands kept a creole language and West African traditions more intact than anywhere else in the country.
For George II, who chartered it in 1732 as a colony for debtors and a buffer against Spanish Florida.
The largest state east of the Mississippi.
Martin Luther King was born in Atlanta, and the state produces most of America’s peanuts and pecans.
From the Alabama people, whose name may mean "clearers of the thicket".
The Montgomery bus boycott began here in 1955 and the Selma marches in 1965; the state is where the civil rights movement was decided.
Rockets for the Apollo programme were designed at Huntsville, which is why it is called Rocket City.
From Ojibwe misi-ziibi, "great river".
The Delta here produced the blues, and Muddy Waters, B.B. King and Robert Johnson all came from within a hundred miles of each other.
Elvis Presley was born in Tupelo, and the state’s catfish farms supply most of the American crop.
From Caddo táysha’, "friend" or "ally", which the Spanish heard as tejas — the state motto is simply "Friendship".
It was an independent republic from 1836 to 1845, and it is the only state that may legally fly its flag at the same height as the national one.
The second largest state, and its economy alone would be among the ten largest countries in the world.
For Louis XIV, named by La Salle when he claimed the whole Mississippi basin for France in 1682.
The only state whose law derives from the Napoleonic Code rather than English common law, so it has parishes rather than counties.
The United States bought it from Napoleon in 1803 for about four cents a hectare, doubling the size of the country.
Spanish for "flowery", named by Ponce de León in 1513 — probably for Pascua Florida, the Easter season, as much as for the vegetation.
The Everglades are a river 100 km wide and 15 cm deep, flowing so slowly it looks like a swamp.
It has the longest coastline in the contiguous states, and more golf courses than any other.
